title: Which prompting strategy is most likely to produce consistent responses across repeated requests?
feedback:
Consistency is improved by using stable prompt structures with clear instructions and well-defined constraints. Provide clear, specific instructions with context.
Source
answer1: Use clear instructions, stable wording, and explicit constraints.
explanation1: Consistent prompts produce more predictable and repeatable outputs.
answer2: Rewrite the prompt differently every time.
explanation2: Changing wording unnecessarily increases output variability.
answer3: Remove all constraints to maximize flexibility.
explanation3: Greater flexibility generally reduces consistency.
answer4: Ask multiple unrelated questions in a single prompt.
explanation4: Combining unrelated requests makes the prompt less focused.

title: What is the best reason to avoid zero-shot prompting when asking for a new team-specific template?
feedback:
When a Scrum Team needs a format that is new or unique to them, examples make the expected pattern clearer than zero-shot instructions alone. Zero-shot prompting relies on internal training knowledge and cannot infer team-specific formats.
Source
answer1: The model has no example of the template to imitate.
explanation1: A new team-specific template requires examples or detailed structure to reduce guesswork.
answer2: Zero-shot prompting cannot generate structured text.
explanation2: Zero-shot prompting can generate structured text, but the structure may not match expectations.
answer3: Zero-shot prompting always produces inaccurate content.
explanation3: It may produce useful content, but accuracy and fit are not guaranteed.
answer4: Zero-shot prompting disables context in the prompt.
explanation4: Context can still be included in a zero-shot prompt.

title: The Scrum Team adds an AI security scanner, but its findings are difficult to explain. What is the most responsible next step?
feedback:
The question focuses on transparency when AI contributes to quality assessment. AI-generated findings should be reviewed and made understandable so the Scrum Team can decide whether they belong in the product's quality expectations. Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.
Source
answer1: Clarify how scanner findings will be reviewed, explained, and reflected in the Definition of Done if relevant.
explanation1: The team should preserve transparency and ensure AI-supported quality checks are understandable and actionable.
answer2: Ignore explanations because automated security tools are usually reliable.
explanation2: Reliability cannot be assumed when findings are unclear or difficult to interpret.
answer3: Treat every AI finding as a blocking defect without discussion.
explanation3: AI findings need human review because they may be false positives or lack context.
answer4: Remove all security checks from the Definition of Done until the tool improves.
explanation4: Removing quality expectations weakens the shared understanding of Done.

title: When evaluating an AI system, which concern most directly reflects ethical AI practice?
feedback:
The question focuses on the ethical consequences of AI use, not the novelty or productivity of the tool. Responsible AI requires inspecting how decisions and outputs may affect people. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Whether the system may create unfair, opaque, unsafe, or unaccountable outcomes.
explanation1: Ethical evaluation should consider fairness, transparency, safety, and responsibility for consequences.
answer2: Whether the system can generate longer answers than previous tools.
explanation2: Output length does not determine whether AI is ethical or safe.
answer3: Whether the system can replace team discussions with automated conclusions.
explanation3: Replacing human judgment can increase ethical and accountability risks.
answer4: Whether the system uses the newest model available from the vendor.
explanation4: A newer model does not automatically make the system responsible or ethical.

title: During preparation for a workshop, the Scrum Master uses AI to suggest icebreakers for a diverse group. What is most important?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master can use AI responsibly in facilitation design. AI may generate useful options, but the Scrum Master must inspect their fit with the group, purpose, and psychological safety. I'm facilitating a cross-cultural session—what icebreakers promote psychological safety?
Source
answer1: Review the suggestions and choose activities that support the workshop purpose and psychological safety.
explanation1: AI-generated ideas must be filtered through human judgment and the needs of the group.
answer2: Use the first AI suggestion to save preparation time.
explanation2: The first suggestion may not fit the group, purpose, or context.
answer3: Let AI randomly assign participants to sensitive discussion groups.
explanation3: Random grouping can create discomfort or reduce safety if context is ignored.
answer4: Allow AI to decide which participants should speak first.
explanation4: Facilitation choices should remain intentional and human-led.

title: A manager wants the Scrum Master to use AI productivity scores to identify underperforming Developers. What should the Scrum Master do first?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master understands that AI metrics can create ethical and cultural risks when used for individual control. The focus should remain on team value, transparency, and responsible accountability. prevent harm, ensure fairness
Source
answer1: Challenge the use of individual AI scores and refocus the discussion on team outcomes and responsible use.
explanation1: The Scrum Master should protect team self-management and avoid reducing complex collaboration to individual AI scores.
answer2: Share the scores with the Product Owner to help reorder the Product Backlog.
explanation2: Individual productivity scores are not a valid basis for Product Backlog ordering.
answer3: Use the scores to assign Sprint Backlog work more efficiently.
explanation3: This undermines self-management and may increase mistrust.
answer4: Tell Developers to accept the scores because AI reduces human bias.
explanation4: AI can still introduce bias and should not replace responsible human judgment.

title: Why is an AI system that detects defects on a production line not an example of AGI?
feedback:
This question tests the distinction between Artificial Narrow Intelligence and Artificial General Intelligence. A system optimized for one bounded task may be useful and advanced, but it is not AGI. single specific task
Source
answer1: It is designed for a specific task rather than broad human-level reasoning.
explanation1: A defect detection system can be valuable, but it remains narrow because its capability is bounded to one purpose.
answer2: It cannot be considered AI unless it uses a Large Language Model.
explanation2: AI is broader than LLMs and can include vision, prediction, classification, and other systems.
answer3: It becomes AGI as soon as it performs better than humans at defect detection.
explanation3: Superior performance in one task does not equal general intelligence.
answer4: It is not AI because it does not produce text or images.
explanation4: AI systems do not need to generate content to be considered AI.

title: Which prompt library design is most useful for repeated Scrum facilitation tasks?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that a useful prompt library should be structured around repeatable needs. Organizing prompts by purpose and using placeholders improves both accessibility and consistency. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Templates organized by facilitation purpose with placeholders for context, audience, and desired output.
explanation1: This structure supports reuse while helping the prompt remain specific to the facilitation situation.
answer2: A collection of unedited AI conversations copied after each Scrum event.
explanation2: Raw conversations are difficult to reuse and may contain irrelevant or sensitive information.
answer3: A single document containing every prompt without labels or structure.
explanation3: Without organization, the library becomes harder to search, maintain, and reuse.
answer4: A private archive controlled only by the Scrum Master.
explanation4: A private archive limits collaboration and prevents the Scrum Team from learning together.

title: Developers want to train an internal AI tool using years of team chat history. What is the most responsible response?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that internal communication data still requires ethical and security safeguards. Responsible AI use should limit collection to a clear purpose and protect people from unnecessary exposure. Responsible & Ethical AI
Source
answer1: Assess purpose, consent, data sensitivity, access control, and retention before using the chat history.
explanation1: Historical chat data may contain personal, confidential, or sensitive information and must be governed carefully.
answer2: Use all available chat history because more data will always improve AI quality.
explanation2: More data can increase risk and does not automatically improve responsible or useful AI outcomes.
answer3: Exclude only messages from external stakeholders and use all internal messages freely.
explanation3: Internal messages may still contain sensitive or personal information.
answer4: Let the AI tool filter inappropriate messages during training.
explanation4: Filtering after the data is provided does not replace prior review, consent, and minimization.

title: The Scrum Team is offered an AI tool that assigns each task to the Developer with the highest predicted efficiency. What is the best concern to discuss?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner sees the difference between optimizing individuals and improving the Scrum Team as a system. AI-driven assignment can appear rational while weakening collective accountability and collaboration. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: The tool may optimize individual efficiency while reducing shared ownership of the Sprint work.
explanation1: The apparent efficiency gain may harm collaboration if Developers no longer manage work together.
answer2: The AI may not format task descriptions according to the team's preferred template.
explanation2: Formatting is not the most important concern when team ownership is at risk.
answer3: The tool may reduce the time needed for Sprint Planning.
explanation3: Reducing planning time is not valuable if it weakens self-management.
answer4: The Product Owner may use the tool to reorder the Product Backlog more frequently.
explanation4: The issue is assignment of Sprint work, not Product Backlog ordering.

title: Which prompting approach best supports AI-assisted analysis of recurring impediments?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands how to prompt AI for careful analysis. Recurring impediments require the Scrum Team to inspect patterns and assumptions, so step-by-step reasoning is more useful than a quick conclusion. Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
Source
answer1: Ask the AI to reason through patterns, possible causes, and evidence before summarizing.
explanation1: This supports structured analysis and helps the team avoid jumping to unsupported conclusions.
answer2: Ask the AI to list the first cause that appears most likely.
explanation2: The first plausible cause may be superficial or unsupported.
answer3: Ask the AI to use a humorous tone to reduce team tension.
explanation3: Tone may help communication, but it does not improve analytical depth.
answer4: Ask the AI to produce a final answer without explaining its assumptions.
explanation4: Without assumptions, the team has less transparency into the analysis.

title: An AI-generated image falsely shows a stakeholder approving a controversial product decision. What is the most responsible next step?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner treats AI-generated media as potentially misleading evidence. Responsible AI use requires verification, accountability, and communication when synthetic content could influence decisions. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Confirm the approval with the stakeholder and correct the misinformation through appropriate channels.
explanation1: This ensures decisions are based on verified information and reduces potential harm from synthetic media.
answer2: Use the image as evidence because it appears realistic.
explanation2: Realistic synthetic content is not reliable evidence of approval.
answer3: Delete the image quietly without informing anyone affected.
explanation3: Silent deletion may leave misinformation uncorrected and reduce transparency.
answer4: Ask another AI system to generate a more accurate version of the image.
explanation4: Generating another image does not verify the underlying approval or correct the risk.

title: A Scrum Team is unsure whether AI-generated refinement notes improve shared understanding. What should they do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the team uses empiricism when evaluating AI. The team should define useful outcomes, test the practice in a low-risk way, and inspect whether shared understanding actually improves. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Define what improvement means, test AI on a small sample, and inspect the outcome together.
explanation1: Clear criteria and shared inspection help the team decide whether the AI practice is valuable.
answer2: Continue using AI until the team becomes comfortable with the tool.
explanation2: Comfort with a tool does not prove that it improves refinement outcomes.
answer3: Ask the AI vendor to confirm whether the feature improves refinement.
explanation3: Vendor claims do not replace the team's own inspection of actual impact.
answer4: Stop all AI experimentation because shared understanding is a human-only activity.
explanation4: AI can assist, but its impact should be tested and inspected responsibly.

title: A Scrum Master starts using AI to prepare facilitation questions and summarize patterns. What remains unchanged?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can separate AI-assisted activities from Scrum Master accountability. Tools may help with preparation or pattern detection, but the Scrum Master still serves the team and organization. Is AI Taking My Job?
Source
answer1: The Scrum Master's accountability for helping the Scrum Team improve its effectiveness.
explanation1: AI can support preparation and analysis, but the Scrum Master remains accountable for enabling improvement.
answer2: The Scrum Master must now accept AI recommendations as final decisions.
explanation2: AI recommendations need human judgment and inspection.
answer3: The Scrum Master should delegate team coaching to the AI assistant.
explanation3: Coaching requires context, trust, and human responsibility that cannot simply be delegated.
answer4: The Scrum Master no longer needs to understand Scrum deeply.
explanation4: AI assistance does not remove the need for strong Scrum understanding.

title: AI proposes adding twenty new checks to the Definition of Done after analyzing past defects. What should the Scrum Team do first?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners understand that AI can help reveal improvement opportunities, but the team must still decide which quality measures belong in Done. A useful Definition of Done should increase transparency and product quality, not simply accumulate controls. If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum.
Source
answer1: Inspect the proposed checks and select only those that meaningfully improve product quality and transparency.
explanation1: The team should evaluate the relevance and value of each proposed check before changing the Definition of Done.
answer2: Adopt all checks because more controls always create higher quality.
explanation2: Too many checks can create waste if they are not relevant or valuable.
answer3: Ask the AI to prioritize the checks and then apply the top five automatically.
explanation3: AI prioritization can help discussion, but it should not replace team judgment.
answer4: Postpone the discussion until the next release because the Definition of Done should not change during development.
explanation4: The Definition of Done can be inspected and adapted when the team learns that quality expectations should change.

title: An AI assistant recommends changing the team's technical approach, but the reasoning is unclear. What should the Scrum Team do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the team treats explainability as part of responsible AI-supported decision-making. When reasoning is unclear, the team should not blindly follow the AI but should inspect the rationale and decide consciously. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Ask for explainable rationale and review the recommendation before deciding.
explanation1: The team should understand the reasoning enough to inspect risks and make an accountable decision.
answer2: Implement the recommendation because AI can process more data than the team.
explanation2: More data does not guarantee a sound recommendation or replace team accountability.
answer3: Escalate the decision to the AI tool administrator.
explanation3: Tool administration does not resolve the need for technical and product judgment.
answer4: Accept the recommendation only if it reduces Sprint workload.
explanation4: Lower workload is not enough if the decision creates risk or weakens quality.

title: A customer-facing chatbot gives regulatory advice that may affect financial decisions. What is the safest responsible design?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can identify safeguards for risky AI advice. When AI output may influence important decisions, the system should make sources visible, clarify limits, and involve humans when needed. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Show source references, include a clear disclaimer, and route high-risk cases to a qualified human.
explanation1: This reduces the chance that users rely blindly on unsupported or incomplete AI-generated advice.
answer2: Increase response speed so users get guidance before they leave the site.
explanation2: Speed does not address accuracy, transparency, or risk.
answer3: Hide source limitations to avoid reducing user trust.
explanation3: Hiding limitations creates false trust and weakens accountability.
answer4: Let the chatbot make final recommendations whenever confidence is high.
explanation4: Confidence does not remove the need for human review in high-risk situations.

title: A Scrum Team asks an AI system to improve onboarding for new Developers. Which response best shows agentic AI?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can recognize agentic AI in a Scrum-related context. The agentic pattern is the ability to manage a process through planning, tool use, feedback, and adaptation. Agentic AI system manages the whole process
Source
answer1: The system identifies onboarding gaps, creates tasks, uses company tools, gathers feedback, and adjusts the plan.
explanation1: This demonstrates planning, tool use, iteration, and goal-directed work across several steps.
answer2: The system writes a single onboarding checklist from one prompt.
explanation2: A single generated checklist is useful but does not show autonomous iteration.
answer3: The system ranks onboarding documents by keyword frequency.
explanation3: Ranking documents is a narrow analytical task, not agentic behavior.
answer4: The system answers questions when a new Developer asks for help.
explanation4: Reactive Q&A alone does not demonstrate autonomous planning toward a broader goal.

title: Which AI system is most clearly an example of Artificial Narrow Intelligence?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that ANI can be powerful and useful while remaining limited to a specific purpose. A recommendation engine is narrow because it solves a defined task rather than demonstrating general intelligence. Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI)
Source
answer1: A recommendation engine that suggests learning resources based on a user's certification goal.
explanation1: This is ANI because it is optimized for a bounded recommendation task within a specific context.
answer2: A system that can learn any profession without task-specific limits.
explanation2: This describes a general-purpose intelligence capability, not ANI.
answer3: An AI that can independently create and validate strategies across every industry.
explanation3: This implies broad cross-domain reasoning, which goes beyond ANI.
answer4: A self-aware digital assistant that decides its own objectives.
explanation4: Self-awareness and independent objectives are not characteristics of ANI.

title: A Scrum Master asks AI to reason through a conflict analysis step by step. What should they remember?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can use Chain-of-Thought responsibly in Scrum Master work. The technique can support analysis, but judgment, context, and accountability remain human. Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
Source
answer1: The reasoning may be useful input, but the Scrum Master must still inspect and validate it.
explanation1: AI-generated reasoning can support reflection, but it should not be treated as definitive truth.
answer2: The step-by-step format proves the analysis is objective.
explanation2: A structured format can still hide bias, missing context, or incorrect assumptions.
answer3: The AI's final conclusion should be accepted if the reasoning sounds coherent.
explanation3: Coherence does not prove that the conclusion is accurate or appropriate.
answer4: The AI becomes accountable for the analysis because it provided reasoning.
explanation4: Accountability remains with people using the AI output.

title: During ideation, Developers disagree and the discussion becomes fragmented. How can AI be used responsibly?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can use AI to improve collaboration without transferring authority to the tool. AI-supported clustering can help the team see patterns, but the Scrum Team must still inspect and decide what matters. brainstorm ideas, outline strategy, facilitate collaboration
Source
answer1: Use AI to cluster the inputs into visible themes that the Scrum Team can review and refine.
explanation1: Clustering helps make the discussion more transparent while keeping interpretation and decisions with the team.
answer2: Let AI remove ideas that appear inconsistent with the majority view.
explanation2: Removing minority views can reduce learning and silence valuable perspectives.
answer3: Ask AI to identify which Developer has the strongest argument.
explanation3: Judging individuals can damage trust and does not support collaborative ideation.
answer4: Let AI produce the final decision because it can process all comments quickly.
explanation4: Fast processing does not replace human accountability for decisions.

title: A Scrum Master wants to understand why similar blockers keep appearing every Sprint. What should AI be used for?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that AI can help with sense-making, not blame assignment. Recurring blockers should be inspected as possible system patterns during the Retrospective. AI-Enhanced Sprint Retrospective
Source
answer1: Cluster recurring blockers and highlight possible systemic themes for the Scrum Team to inspect.
explanation1: Clustering helps reveal patterns without turning AI into the owner of conclusions or actions.
answer2: Generate a list of underperforming team members linked to each blocker.
explanation2: This creates a blame-oriented use of AI and does not help the team inspect systemic causes.
answer3: Automatically route each blocker to the Developer with the closest skill match.
explanation3: Routing blockers automatically may reduce shared ownership and avoid root-cause discussion.
answer4: Remove minor recurring blockers from the analysis to protect team morale.
explanation4: Minor recurring blockers may still indicate an important systemic issue.

title: Before a Retrospective, AI detects a recurring theme of low trust in team survey responses. What should the Scrum Master do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master can use AI-supported insights without creating false certainty or blame. When AI surfaces a sensitive theme, the Scrum Master should preserve safety and let the team inspect the signal together. Keeping psychological safety high is a must.
Source
answer1: Use the theme carefully as input and create space for the team to validate or reframe it.
explanation1: Sensitive AI-detected themes should be handled with care and discussed by the team, not imposed as fact.
answer2: Announce that the AI has confirmed trust is the team's main problem.
explanation2: AI output should not be presented as confirmed truth, especially on sensitive topics.
answer3: Ask AI to identify which team members caused the trust issue.
explanation3: Attributing sensitive themes to individuals can damage psychological safety.
answer4: Remove the theme from the agenda because trust is too difficult to discuss.
explanation4: Avoiding the topic may prevent meaningful inspection and improvement.

title: An AI tool produces a well-written customer trend report, but the sources are missing. What is the most appropriate response?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Team understands that missing sources are a risk signal. A well-written AI report should remain provisional until important claims are verified. Using AI responsibly and ethically is mandatory to prevent harm, ensure fairness, and maintain public trust.
Source
answer1: Treat the report as unverified and validate key claims before using it.
explanation1: Without sources, the team cannot know whether the claims are accurate, current, or relevant.
answer2: Use the report because the writing quality suggests strong reasoning.
explanation2: Writing quality does not provide evidence that the claims are true.
answer3: Ask the AI to add citations after the report has already been accepted.
explanation3: Citations should be verified before the report is accepted or used.
answer4: Use the report only for internal decisions because stakeholders will not see it.
explanation4: Internal decisions can still create product risk if based on incorrect information.

title: Which explanation best fits backpropagation in simple terms?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can explain backpropagation without confusing it with retrieval, memorization, or human review. Backpropagation is about using error signals to improve model parameters. Backpropagation
Source
answer1: The model works backward from an error to adjust the internal weights that contributed to it.
explanation1: Backpropagation propagates error information backward through the network to guide weight updates.
answer2: The model searches the internet to find a more accurate answer.
explanation2: Searching external sources is retrieval, not backpropagation.
answer3: The model stores every training example so it can copy the closest answer later.
explanation3: Backpropagation updates parameters; it does not simply memorize and copy examples.
answer4: The model asks a human to correct each output before continuing.
explanation4: Human correction can support training data quality, but backpropagation itself is an algorithmic training process.

title: A Developer suggests using AI to summarize technical discussions for one Sprint. What should the Scrum Team do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the team experiments safely with AI before institutionalizing a practice. A limited trial helps reveal benefits, risks, and effects on collaboration. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: Try it as a limited experiment and inspect whether it improves shared understanding.
explanation1: A bounded experiment lets the team evaluate usefulness without committing to a permanent practice.
answer2: Use the summaries as the official source of truth immediately.
explanation2: AI summaries may miss nuance and should not become authoritative without inspection.
answer3: Reject the idea because AI should not influence team collaboration.
explanation3: AI can support collaboration when used responsibly and inspected by the team.
answer4: Expand the practice to all meetings before measuring results.
explanation4: Scaling before inspection increases risk and reduces learning.

title: During refinement, AI generates several acceptance criteria for a Product Backlog item. Some are useful, while others add unnecessary scope. What should happen next?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners can filter AI-generated refinement output responsibly. Acceptance criteria should clarify expectations, not automatically expand scope or replace product judgment. Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.
Source
answer1: Discuss the suggestions and keep only the criteria that improve clarity without adding unjustified scope.
explanation1: The Scrum Team should inspect AI output and ensure it supports the intended product outcome.
answer2: Accept all AI-generated criteria because more detail always improves refinement quality.
explanation2: More detail can create waste or increase scope without improving value.
answer3: Let the AI decide which criteria are mandatory based on similar products.
explanation3: The AI lacks full product context and cannot own the team's refinement decisions.
answer4: Remove all AI-generated criteria because acceptance criteria must be written manually.
explanation4: Rejecting all AI help ignores potentially useful support that can be inspected by the team.

title: A Product Owner uses AI to summarize stakeholder feedback before refinement. What should happen before the summary influences Product Backlog items?
feedback:
This question checks whether AI-generated refinement preparation is treated as provisional input. Before changing the Product Backlog, the Scrum Team should validate whether the AI summary reflects the real stakeholder feedback. Product Backlog refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller more precise items.
Source
answer1: The Product Owner and Scrum Team should review the summary for accuracy, missing context, and relevance.
explanation1: AI summaries can miss nuance, so the team should validate them before using them to shape Product Backlog items.
answer2: The summary should be accepted if it is concise and well formatted.
explanation2: Concise formatting does not prove the summary is accurate or complete.
answer3: The AI should automatically create and order new Product Backlog items from the summary.
explanation3: AI can assist drafting, but ordering and accountability remain human responsibilities.
answer4: The Developers should skip the feedback and work only from AI-generated acceptance criteria.
explanation4: AI-generated criteria do not replace shared understanding of stakeholder needs.

title: AI-generated Sprint Goals vary too much from one Sprint to another. Which prompting technique should the Scrum Master try first?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands that inconsistent output format can often be improved by providing examples. Few-shot prompting demonstrates the pattern the AI should follow. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Add examples of past Sprint Goals that represent the desired output.
explanation1: Past examples reduce variability by showing the model what a good answer should look like.
answer2: Increase the model's creativity so it can produce more original Sprint Goals.
explanation2: More creativity may increase variation rather than consistency.
answer3: Remove constraints so the AI can find the best wording independently.
explanation3: Removing constraints makes the output less predictable.
answer4: Ask AI to write a longer explanation before producing the Sprint Goal.
explanation4: A longer explanation does not necessarily improve format consistency.

title: What problem does Retrieval-Augmented Generation primarily address for LLM-based knowledge tools?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands the main limitation RAG is meant to reduce. It helps an LLM answer using relevant retrieved information rather than relying only on what is already in the model. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: The need to ground answers in relevant information beyond the model's original training data.
explanation1: RAG helps connect generation to retrieved information, which is useful when knowledge changes or is organization-specific.
answer2: The need to make every answer more creative.
explanation2: RAG is about grounding and retrieval, not maximizing creativity.
answer3: The need to remove human review from high-risk answers.
explanation3: RAG can improve grounding, but human review may still be needed for high-risk outputs.
answer4: The need to make a smaller model as capable as a larger one.
explanation4: RAG does not simply replace model capability with model compression.

title: A Scrum Master wants AI-generated stakeholder updates to follow the same template each Sprint. What should the prompt include?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner knows when examples are needed. If the team wants the same stakeholder update template every Sprint, few-shot prompting is more suitable than generic instructions. Few-Shot Prompting
Source
answer1: Several sample updates that already follow the desired stakeholder update template.
explanation1: Sample outputs teach the model the structure, tone, and content boundaries expected in the answer.
answer2: A broad request to summarize Sprint progress clearly.
explanation2: A broad request may produce useful content, but it does not reliably enforce the team’s template.
answer3: A high-level persona such as 'Act as a stakeholder communication expert'.
explanation3: A persona can shape style, but it does not demonstrate the required format.
answer4: A request for the AI to vary the format to avoid repetition.
explanation4: Varying the format is the opposite of the desired consistency.

title: Developers begin asking AI to settle disagreements about design trade-offs. What is the most important risk?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners understand that technical disagreement can be valuable for team learning. AI can help explore options, but it should not short-circuit the team's shared understanding or accountability. The A3 Framework: Assist, Automate, Avoid - A Decision System for AI Delegation
Source
answer1: AI may stop the team from building shared understanding of the trade-offs.
explanation1: Design decisions need discussion because the team must understand and own the implications.
answer2: AI may not know the team's preferred naming conventions.
explanation2: Naming conventions are less important than losing shared understanding of technical choices.
answer3: The AI output may be too long to review quickly.
explanation3: Review effort is not the main concern when team decision-making is being bypassed.
answer4: Stakeholders may want to see the AI transcript.
explanation4: Stakeholder visibility is not the primary issue in technical self-management.

title: An AI assistant gives generic Retrospective suggestions that do not reflect the team's recent discussions. What should be changed?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands the cause of generic AI advice. When the model lacks the team's actual context, RAG can supply relevant notes before generation. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Connect the AI to the team's Retrospective notes through a retrieval-augmented approach.
explanation1: RAG can provide the model with relevant team-specific notes so the response reflects the real context.
answer2: Increase the model's creativity so it generates more surprising suggestions.
explanation2: Creativity may produce novelty, but it does not make the response grounded in actual team evidence.
answer3: Use a single persona prompt to make the AI sound more like a facilitator.
explanation3: A persona can influence tone, but it does not provide the missing team data.
answer4: Ask for shorter recommendations so the team can review them faster.
explanation4: Shorter recommendations may still be generic if the AI lacks the team's notes.

title: A Scrum Team is building an AI knowledge base for internal product policies. What design choice best improves reliability?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners understand that internal policy answers require grounding in approved sources. RAG is appropriate because it combines document retrieval with generated responses. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
Source
answer1: Connect the LLM to indexed policy documents through retrieval-augmented generation.
explanation1: This lets the assistant use relevant policy sources before producing an answer.
answer2: Use only a larger LLM to reduce the need for document retrieval.
explanation2: A larger model still may not know current internal policies or provide source-grounded answers.
answer3: Ask users to paste policy documents manually into every prompt.
explanation3: Manual pasting is inconsistent, inefficient, and prone to missing relevant context.
answer4: Generate policy answers first and search documents only when users challenge them.
explanation4: Verification should be built into the answering process, not added only after disputes.

title: A new Scrum Team wants to explore AI but is unsure where to begin. What approach best balances learning and safety?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner understands AI adoption as an empirical team capability. A low-risk experiment with explicit learning goals helps the team gain experience while keeping the impact inspectable. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Choose one low-risk use case, define what the team wants to learn, and inspect it in the Retrospective.
explanation1: This creates a safe learning loop and avoids overwhelming the team with broad AI adoption.
answer2: Adopt the most advanced AI tool available and apply it across all work immediately.
explanation2: Advanced tools do not guarantee value and may increase confusion for a new team.
answer3: Ask management to select the AI practices the team must follow.
explanation3: Top-down selection weakens team ownership and may not match the team's real needs.
answer4: Postpone AI until the team has completed several releases without problems.
explanation4: A team can learn responsibly without waiting for perfect maturity or problem-free releases.

title: The Scrum Team receives an AI-generated proposal that sounds balanced but reflects only the sponsor's priorities. What should they change in the prompt?
feedback:
This question checks whether the learner can diagnose a prompt that produces a one-sided proposal. To improve the output, the prompt should explicitly ask for contrasting stakeholder perspectives. Generate multiple distinct possibilities
Source
answer1: Request contrasting perspectives from users, sponsors, Developers, and risk-focused stakeholders.
explanation1: The prompt should explicitly broaden the viewpoints so the output does not overfit one stakeholder group.
answer2: Ask the AI to make the sponsor perspective more detailed.
explanation2: More detail from one perspective does not solve the lack of perspective diversity.
answer3: Ask the AI to shorten the proposal so it is easier to read.
explanation3: A shorter answer may still be biased toward one viewpoint.
answer4: Ask the AI to use a more neutral tone.
explanation4: Neutral tone does not guarantee that missing perspectives are included.

title: A Scrum Team's AI-generated user stories vary in role, benefit statement, and acceptance criteria depth. What should they do?
feedback:
This question checks whether the team can use prompt standardization to improve consistency. When the expected user story format matters, the prompt should explicitly define the structure and quality expectations. Prompt Library for Facilitators
Source
answer1: Agree on a shared prompt pattern that defines role, goal, benefit, and criteria expectations.
explanation1: A shared pattern helps the team generate outputs that support consistent refinement and discussion.
answer2: Let every Developer keep their own format to encourage creativity.
explanation2: Creativity may be useful, but uncontrolled variation can make refinement harder.
answer3: Ask the Product Owner to rewrite every AI-generated story manually.
explanation3: Manual rewriting treats the symptom rather than improving the team's prompting practice.
answer4: Use zero-shot prompting so the model can freely infer the best format.
explanation4: Zero-shot prompting is weaker when the team needs a specific repeated structure.

title: A Scrum Master asks AI for a plan to address a recurring blocker. One step seems inconsistent with the team's working agreements. What should happen?
feedback:
This question checks whether the Scrum Master keeps team agreements and human accountability central. AI may suggest useful actions, but recommendations must be validated against the team's current agreements and context. Assist (AI drafts, you actively review and decide)
Source
answer1: Review the step with the team and validate whether it aligns with current agreements before applying it.
explanation1: AI output should be inspected against the team's real context before any change is introduced.
answer2: Apply the step because AI-generated plans are designed to optimize team effectiveness.
explanation2: Optimization claims do not remove the need for human inspection and agreement.
answer3: Ask the AI to decide whether the working agreement should be ignored.
explanation3: AI should not decide whether the team bypasses its own agreements.
answer4: Replace all working agreements with the AI-generated plan to avoid inconsistency.
explanation4: The team's agreements should not be replaced automatically by AI output.

title: AI-generated backlog summaries make refinement faster, but Developers report weaker understanding of upcoming work. What should be prioritized?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners distinguish efficiency from effectiveness. AI may reduce meeting time, but if it weakens Developers' understanding, the Scrum Team should inspect and adapt. The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.
Source
answer1: Restore shared understanding by adapting the AI practice, even if refinement becomes less fast.
explanation1: The goal is not only speed; refinement should increase understanding and confidence in Product Backlog items.
answer2: Keep the practice unchanged because faster refinement is evidence of success.
explanation2: Speed alone does not prove that refinement is effective or valuable.
answer3: Ask AI to generate more detailed technical notes for Developers.
explanation3: More AI-generated detail may not restore team conversation or ownership.
answer4: Move refinement ownership entirely to the Product Owner.
explanation4: The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog, but refinement benefits from Scrum Team collaboration.

title: A Scrum Team receives an AI-generated proposal to change service terms that affect customers. What should they avoid?
feedback:
This question checks whether learners can identify the unsafe pattern: moving from AI-generated suggestion directly to implementation. Responsible AI use keeps humans accountable for high-impact policy decisions. Avoid (AI stays out; humans decide and act)
Source
answer1: Allowing the AI proposal to be implemented without formal review and stakeholder input.
explanation1: AI-generated proposals with customer impact require human accountability and stakeholder consultation before implementation.
answer2: Treating the AI proposal as an option to inspect.
explanation2: This is appropriate because AI output can be useful as input for human review.
answer3: Checking whether the proposal creates compliance or fairness risks.
explanation3: This is appropriate because policy changes can create ethical and legal consequences.
answer4: Discussing the proposal with affected stakeholders before deciding.
explanation4: Stakeholder input is appropriate when changes affect customer expectations or outcomes.
